title: Best Cricket Bats for Beginners in India (2026)
summary: Three cricket bats for beginners in India from Cosco, SG and SS: tennis ball, Kashmir willow and English willow. Based on maker pages.
description: Helps first-time buyers in India choose a cricket bat for tennis ball or leather ball. 3 picks from Cosco, SG and SS, with plain tips on wood, size and care.
lead: Which cricket bat should a beginner buy in India? It depends on the ball you will play with. This guide has three picks from three Indian brands. One is a Cosco bat that the maker says is suitable for a cricket tennis ball. One is an SG Kashmir willow bat that the maker lists for a leather ball. One is an SS English willow bat. We read each maker's own product page and we say what those pages do not tell you. In our view, the Budget, Mid-range and Premium tags are a rough guide to the class of bat. For general advice we use Wikipedia and CHOICE (Australia), writing about junior bats, in a guide last updated in 2018.

picks.name: Cosco Striker Cricket Bat (Kashmir willow, for tennis ball)
picks.label: Tennis ball, per maker
picks.verdict: A Cosco bat that the maker says is suitable for a cricket tennis ball. The maker's page gives a weight, but not the length or handle details.
paragraphs: Cosco's own store page for the Striker says it is made with a custom selected Kashmir willow and is suitable for a cricket tennis ball. The page lists sizes 4, 5, 6 and Full. It gives a weight of around 1144 grams. It does not say which size that weight is for. The maker says the bat is hand crafted by artisanal craftsmen to ensure good balance and light weight. That is the maker's claim.
The page does not give the length or handle details. The maker names the tennis ball only, and does not list this bat for a leather ball.
good: The maker says it is suitable for a cricket tennis ball.
Four sizes are listed (4, 5, 6 and Full).
The page names the wood (Kashmir willow) and gives a weight of around 1144 g.
not_good: The page does not say which size the weight is for, and gives no length.
The page gives no handle details.
The maker names the tennis ball only and does not list it for a leather ball.

picks.name: SG Scorer Classic Kashmir Willow Cricket Bat
picks.label: Leather ball, per maker
picks.verdict: A Kashmir willow bat that the maker lists for a leather ball, with a full-length cover and size and weight details. SG's page gives suitability as age 15+ and height 5 ft 6 in and above.
paragraphs: SG's own store page lists the Scorer Classic as Kashmir willow, hard pressed and traditionally shaped. It gives the ball type as leather. The full-size bat is 33.7 inches (85.7 cm) long and weighs 1170 to 1220 g. The page also lists smaller sizes 3, 4, 5 and 6, with lengths of 72, 74, 78 and 80 cm, and an SH size of 85 cm.

The handle is Singapore cane with a special 3-way insertion of rubber between the splits. The maker describes it as a traditional round cane handle for supreme grip and overall bat control. The toe is flat. A full-length bat cover is included. SG's page gives suitability as age 15+ and height 5 ft 6 in and above.
good: The maker lists it for a leather ball.
Weight, length, handle and toe type are all stated on the maker's page.
A full-length bat cover is included, says the maker.
Smaller sizes are listed with their lengths.
not_good: CHOICE says Kashmir willow is harder, denser and less springy than English willow.
In our view, at 1170 to 1220 g the full size may be heavy for a smaller player. CHOICE, writing about children's bats, says balance and pick-up matter more than weight.
SG's page gives suitability as age 15+ and height 5 ft 6 in and above.
picks.search_query: SG Scorer Classic Kashmir willow cricket bat

picks.name: SS Master-500 English Willow Cricket Bat
picks.label: English willow, per maker
picks.verdict: An English willow bat from SS Cricket, made by Sareen Sports Industries per the page, with a cover. The maker's page does not give weight or ball type.
paragraphs: SS's official store page lists the Master-500 as English willow in a naturally patterned Butterfly Grade. The maker says the willow is air-dried and has straight, evenly spaced grains. It describes a modern design with concave edges, a rounded or flat toe and a cover. The page says it is manufactured, marketed and packed by Sareen Sports Industries, with an address in Meerut, India, and gives the country of origin as India. The only size shown is SH (short handle).

The page does not say which ball the bat is for, and it gives no weight or length. It does not say what Butterfly Grade means. It also does not say if the bat is knocked in or oiled. Wikipedia says bats require knocking-in to allow the soft fibres to strike a hard new cricket ball. CHOICE says a bat labelled pre-prepared or "ready to play" has had its initial knocking-in done. In our view, check with the seller or maker before you use it.
good: It is English willow, which CHOICE calls the best type.
The maker says the willow is air-dried and has straight, evenly spaced grains.
A cover is listed with the bat.
The page names the maker (Sareen Sports Industries, Meerut) and gives the country of origin as India.
not_good: No weight, length or ball type is stated on the page.
The page does not explain Butterfly Grade or say if the bat is ready to play.
Only the SH (short handle) size is listed.

choose.heading: Match the bat to the ball
choose.text: In our view, use the ball the maker names. Cosco says the Striker suits a tennis ball. SG lists the Scorer Classic for a leather ball. The SS page does not name a ball. Wikipedia says bats require knocking-in to allow the soft fibres to strike a hard new cricket ball.

choose.heading: Kashmir willow or English willow
choose.text: CHOICE says English willow is the best type. It says Kashmir willow is harder and denser, less springy, and harder wearing, which is why many junior bats use it. Wikipedia takes a different view. It says Kashmir willow is the same species as English willow and says no evidence has been presented that the wood or finished product has different properties. It also says much of the English willow bat market consists of bats made in India from imported English willow blanks, and that it would be virtually impossible to detect counterfeit English willow bats made from Kashmir willow. In our view, read the wood line on the maker's page.

choose.heading: Size and fit
choose.text: CHOICE, writing about children's bats, says to take your batting stance with the toe of the bat resting against the outside of your back foot. The top of the handle should rest against the inside groin of your front leg. It warns against buying a bigger bat to grow into, as it could be too long or heavy and frustrate play. SG lists lengths of 72, 74, 78 and 80 cm for sizes 3 to 6, and 85 cm for SH.

choose.heading: Weight and pick-up
choose.text: CHOICE says the balance, pick-up and overall feel of a bat matter more than its weight. CHOICE, writing about children's bats, says to get your child to hold the bat at arm's length with their top hand, and that if they cannot hold it comfortably the bat is too heavy for them. Wikipedia also calls the pick-up, or weight distribution, of a bat important. Of our three picks, SG gives a weight range, Cosco gives one figure of around 1144 g, and SS gives none.

choose.heading: Knocking-in and oiling
choose.text: CHOICE says to lightly hit the face and edges of a new bat with an old leather ball or a bat mallet, to toughen the wood. It also says linseed oil helps protect the wood, but you can overdo it, so get expert advice. CHOICE says a bat labelled pre-prepared or "ready to play" has had its initial knocking-in done. Wikipedia describes the same two steps. None of the three maker pages we read says if its bat comes ready to play.

choose.heading: Grades and size limits
choose.text: Wikipedia says bats with 8 or fewer grains on the face are held to be harder and take longer to play well, but also to last longer. Bats with 16 or more grains are held to be softer and more playable immediately, with a reduced lifespan. It calls 8 to 12 grains the commonly desired range. The SS page names a Butterfly Grade and does not explain it. For size limits, Wikipedia says the Laws allow a bat up to 38 inches (96.5 cm) long and 4.25 inches (10.8 cm) wide. In our view, check the model name, size and wood against the maker's page.

faq.q: Can I use a tennis-ball bat with a leather ball?
faq.a: In our view, use the ball the maker names. Cosco names the tennis ball for the Striker and does not list it for a leather ball. Wikipedia says bats require knocking-in to allow the soft fibres to strike a hard new cricket ball.

faq.q: Is Kashmir willow or English willow better for a beginner?
faq.a: CHOICE calls English willow the best type. It says Kashmir willow is harder, denser and less springy, and harder wearing, and many junior bats use it. Wikipedia says no evidence has been presented that the wood or finished product has different properties. In our view, Kashmir willow is a reasonable first wood for a beginner.

faq.q: What size cricket bat should I buy?
faq.a: In our view, go by fit. CHOICE, writing about children's bats, says to rest the toe against your back foot, so the top of the handle reaches the inside groin of your front leg. It warns against buying a bigger bat to grow into, as it could be too long or heavy and frustrate play. SG's page gives suitability for the Scorer Classic as age 15+ and height 5 ft 6 in and above.

faq.q: Do I need to knock in a new bat?
faq.a: CHOICE describes knocking-in the face and edges by lightly hitting them with an old leather ball or a bat mallet, and says a bat labelled pre-prepared or "ready to play" has had its initial knocking-in done. The maker pages we read do not say if their bats are ready to play. In our view, check with the seller or maker before you use one.

faq.q: What do the grades on English willow bats mean?
faq.a: Wikipedia describes quality by the number of grains on the face. It says bats with 8 or fewer grains are held to be harder and take longer to play well, but also to last longer, and bats with 16 or more are held to be softer and more playable immediately, with a reduced lifespan. The SS page names Butterfly Grade but does not explain it. In our view, check what it means with the maker.

faq.q: How long can a cricket bat be?
faq.a: Wikipedia says the Laws of Cricket allow a bat up to 38 inches (96.5 cm) long and 4.25 inches (10.8 cm) wide.
